title: State tax agencies use machine-learning models to score returns and select audits
problem: State agencies cannot manually review the millions of returns they receive; for a private multistate company, selection criteria are unpublished and taxpayers have few tools to challenge being selected.
approach: South Carolina's revenue department signed a $3.5 million, five-year contract with FAST Enterprises for audit services that suggest where audits should happen.
Tax Notes reports California began using machine-learning models in 2021 to pick returns; New York says its system is not AI.
In a 2025 Tax Notes survey, 7 of 36 responding state agencies reported using AI (independent); audit-yield and false-positive figures are unpublished.
South Carolina's system suggests audits and auditors conduct them; in California, flagged items go to staff or further automated systems.
who: South Carolina, California, New York tax agencies

title: States match third-party data with filings to find unregistered businesses and non-filers
problem: A growing company can create state tax obligations where it is not registered; commentary says states are getting better at spotting this by linking siloed data.
approach: The Sales Tax Institute says AI improves audit selection and uncovers unregistered remote sellers by linking siloed data (webinar listing).
A consultancy blog lists signals it says states weigh: processor totals against reported sales, marketplace reports, nexus thresholds, exemption certificate gaps.
Withum's recap says officials from eight Southeastern states described AI and analytics for risk identification, audit selection and fraud detection.
No state publishes detection yield in the sources read, and none describes how agency staff review flags.
who: Sales Tax Institute, Withum, a tax consultancy

title: Residency and remote-worker tax audits use analytics and mass letters (New York)
problem: Remote workers in a low-tax state for a high-tax-state employer, and people claiming a residency change, create income tax and withholding exposure for private-company owners and employers.
approach: A 2024 Business Insider article says New York has been sending hundreds of thousands of AI-generated letters, mostly to wealthy remote workers.
A SALT lawyer told CNBC that tax departments use auditors and AI to examine cellphone records to see where people spend time.
New York's department says its selection system is not AI, so the AI label is disputed.
New York reported 771,000 audits in 2022, up 56%, with auditors down 5% to under 200 (self-reported); the AI share is unclear.
who: New York tax department, Business Insider, CNBC

title: AI-assisted multistate nexus study with state-by-state verification
problem: A nexus study asks, state by state and tax by tax, whether sales, property, payroll or people create a filing duty, using thresholds that keep changing.
approach: Kintsugi and Truss advertise a webinar showing live examples of AI agents answering nexus questions across a client portfolio and state thresholds.
Thomson Reuters lists CoCounsel Tax nexus templates, including remote-employee risk and state-by-state economic nexus; no customer use is described.
A law-firm article says the practitioner must independently verify sales and transaction thresholds, tax rates and effective dates state by state.
Mercor seeks state tax experts to evaluate and correct AI nexus answers; no outcome figures are published.

title: Platforms and agents handle state registrations triggered by a remote hire
problem: One employee working in a new state can require a foreign qualification, a withholding account, an unemployment insurance registration and other agency accounts before payroll can run there.
approach: Gusto announced it acquired Mosey, an AI-powered state and local registration platform; Gusto Business Compliance is expected later in 2026.
Warp says its AI agents open state tax accounts and file payroll forms once a customer enters a new employee's work state.
Skyvern says its AI works through state registration portals in parallel, against a manual baseline of 15-30 minutes per state (vendor-published).
No accuracy or penalty figures are published; a human checkpoint is not described for registrations.

title: Apportionment factors computed from reconciled ledgers by rules, with optional AI commentary
problem: Sales, payroll and property factors are often computed separately by entity, creating reconciliation work and error risk when state returns are prepared.
approach: Alteryx's starter kit reconciles factor inputs from source systems, applies jurisdiction rules and checks factors across jurisdictions and against prior periods.
It builds an audit trail from each filed factor to its source; guidance covers feeding output to a language model for commentary.
The core calculation is rules-based; CCH announced a rules-based suite in 2014. No customer, accuracy or time-saving figure is published (vendor-published).
Prior-period anomalies are surfaced for explanation before filing.

title: AI research assistants for multi-jurisdiction state tax questions, with authorities checked
problem: State answers differ by state and year, so a wrong or stale citation changes the advice (for 2025, New York's pass-through credit is refundable; California's is not).
approach: Thomson Reuters says its Checkpoint Catalyst state topics integrate into CoCounsel Tax; Blue J's platform supports federal, state and local tax research.
COST's March 2026 workshop scheduled demonstrations of embedded research tools such as Bloomberg AI and Checkpoint CoCounsel.
On a public Vals benchmark state tax question, one of 18 models passed all checks; twelve scored 0 (independent).
On Vals' broader, mostly federal Tax Agent Bench the best model scored 49.19% (independent); the practitioner verifies authorities and effective dates.
who: Thomson Reuters, Blue J, Vals, COST

title: Idea: in-house state tax team uses AI for quarterly updates, bill comparisons
problem: Idea, not a deployment: state tax teams track many bills, rulings and cases and write periodic updates, and the law moves fast.
approach: Idea: a COST workshop agenda listed demonstrations of AI drafting quarterly state tax updates, comparing legislative proposal versions and reviewing appeal arguments.
The demonstrations were to be presented by staff from AT&T, EY and Reed Smith; nothing shows a team doing this in production.
No outcome figures or human checkpoints are described.

title: Idea: self-scan for the signals states match on, before a notice arrives
problem: Idea, not a deployment: if states link filing, marketplace and payment data, companies that have never reconciled their own footprint have exposure they cannot see.
approach: Idea: review nexus footprint, exemption certificates, product taxability and under-collected periods before a state does (consultancy suggestion).
The Sales Tax Institute says its webinar will cover responding when nexus is triggered, addressing historical exposure early and strengthening data controls.
Withum advises periodic tax health checks; none of the three sources describes a deployed AI scan.
A professional decides on registration and disclosure; the consultancy says AI cannot register, fix past periods or make judgment calls.

title: Idea: defending AI-informed state assessments with analytics, transparent documentation and human judgment
problem: Idea, not a deployment: if an assessment starts from an opaque model score, the taxpayer must answer it without knowing what triggered it.
approach: Akerman announced a partner would present at COST's 57th Annual Meeting on defending AI-driven state assessments.
The proposed approach combines data analytics, transparent documentation and human judgment.
The announcement describes the session, not a method used on a case; no outcomes are published.

title: Voluntary disclosure and exposure review marketed against state AI detection
problem: Companies with unregistered states must choose between voluntary disclosure (reduced penalties; a consultancy says often a two-to-four-year lookback, only before an audit opens), amnesty or waiting.
approach: A sales-tax consultancy argues that disclosing before a state's AI flags the business is cheaper than an audit afterwards.
The service is human; the AI link is only the argument that detection is getting cheaper.
Independent: the Multistate Tax Commission's program had 464 executed agreements and $28,308,873 collected in fiscal 2026, averaging $61,010 each.
Professional-led negotiation; no AI step is described.
who: Multistate Tax Commission, a sales-tax consultancy

title: Idea: outside review, inventories and bias testing of state audit-selection models
problem: Idea, not a deployment: in cases Tax Notes examined, selection systems got only internal review, and oversight laws miss systems not classified as AI or high risk.
approach: Idea: experts quoted by Tax Notes say agencies should have outside oversight from lawmakers, another agency or a state auditor.
A Stanford researcher wants clear goals so systems avoid disproportionately selecting lower-income taxpayers, yet sees machine learning as potentially good against bias.
A vendor executive urges continuous testing, logging of model inputs and outputs, and documented decision rules for revenue-agency AI pilots.
New York's Comptroller 2025 audit of four non-tax agencies found no statewide AI inventory and inadequate central guidance.
who: Tax Notes, Stanford researcher, NY Comptroller

title: AI companies as a new state tax client segment for mid-market firms
problem: Fast-growing AI companies sell into many states, hire remotely and sell products that states classify differently, which can trigger sales and use, income, franchise, gross receipts and payroll obligations.
approach: This is demand created by AI, not AI used in the tax work.
Moss Adams published state tax guidance for AI companies in April 2025 and ran a webinar in August 2025.
Checkpoint says Maryland, Texas and Washington extended sales taxes to various automated services, and states will struggle to classify generative AI.
No client count, revenue or engagement figure is published (self-reported); the service is professional advice.
who: Moss Adams, Thomson Reuters Checkpoint, Eide Bailly

title: Pass-through entity tax election modelling for owners, with each state's treatment checked
problem: Owners hear that a pass-through entity tax election saves tax and want to know if it is worth it; Gelt says most online calculators suit only simple W-2 cases.
approach: Gelt, an AI-native tax firm, launched a hub of AI-powered calculators on 29 December 2025, including a pass-through entity tax calculator.
Gelt says owners can move from estimate to expert execution with the firm; no conversion figure is published (vendor-published).
Filed shows a sample planning report with a Maryland election and an illustrative saving of $22,222 per year (not a client result).
The adviser confirms facts, each state's treatment and the assumptions behind any savings figure before it reaches the owner.
